brief:
In the lanes of Old Askar camp, on the eastern edge of Nablus, the idea started as the kind of question men ask each other when they already know the answer is no.

Why, a few members of the camp's popular committee asked, does a camp this size not own an ambulance?

Hatem al-Hafi, who handles the international relations file for the Popular Committee for Services of Old Askar Camp, told the camp news platform From the Camp that the question sounded mad when it was first said out loud. Within roughly a year it had a chassis, a crew and an intensive-care unit bolted inside.

The money came from Boulder, Colorado, almost 11,000 kilometres away.

## The camp that had no ambulance

UNRWA's camp profile, updated in January with 2025 figures, registers 25,446 Palestine refugees in Askar camp, on 0.119 square kilometres — about 119 dunams. That makes it, the agency says, among the most densely populated camps in the occupied West Bank, where overcrowding and unemployment are the most serious problems.

UNRWA runs six schools and two health centres in the camp. It also notes something that matters more to this story than any of its figures: Askar has an active civil society with numerous community-based organisations.

One of them spent 2023 looking at a problem of geography. Essrea Cherin, co-founder of the Boulder-Nablus Sister City Project, put it to the Denver television station Denver7 in a single sentence: "The eastern side of the city of Nablus doesn't have any hospitals."

Ambulances had to come from the western side of the city and cross Israeli closures to reach the eastern camps. Families who could not wait drove the wounded in private cars, which soldiers stop more readily than they stop an ambulance.

Al-Hafi described the sharper version of that problem to From the Camp. When the army raids the camp, outside crews are kept out altogether.

## A town that keeps a ledger

The Boulder-Nablus Sister City Project was founded in 2011, and Rocky Mountain PBS put its membership at around 70 people, most of them in Boulder County. In May 2017, the project says, the mayors of Nablus and Boulder signed a partnership agreement between the two cities.

Its first purchase was modest: $15,000 for an incubator for a Palestinian hospital, according to Denver7. The ambulance was not chosen in Colorado. It was chosen in Askar, when a Boulder delegation sat with camp representatives and asked what was needed next.

The group expected the $75,000 to take years and raised it in nine months, Denver7 reported. The vehicle was built in Turkey, where al-Hafi said prices had fallen after the 2023 earthquake left medical suppliers holding stock they could not sell, and the manufacturer took $17,000 off the price.

A shipping company then carried it for nothing. Cherin said the freight would normally have cost "five or $7,000". It sailed on 2 May — the day before Turkey halted its trade with Israel.

> "This isn't really a divisive idea. Anyone can get behind saving lives with an ambulance."
> Essrea Cherin, co-founder of the Boulder-Nablus Sister City Project, to Denver7

## Forty-five volunteers and a nominal fee

What arrived in Askar was rare in Palestine: an ambulance carrying an intensive-care unit, able to take a critical case rather than only carry it. Forty-five volunteers staff the camp's ambulance centre, From the Camp reported.

During incursions the vehicle works when other crews cannot reach the alleys. The rest of the time it answers the camp's ordinary emergencies for a nominal fee, which covers maintenance and running costs.

That small detail is the part most donated equipment never has. The committee decided at the outset who would pay for the ambulance in its third year, and built the answer into the way it is used.

![What Boulder sent to Askar camp: fifteen years of deliveries, set beside UNRWA's figures for the camp](times-of-palestine-diaspora-dispatch-2026-11-27-boulder-askar.svg)

## The clinic, opened on a Wednesday in November

The delegates who came to hand over the ambulance left with the next request. The camp wanted a clinic, because the UNRWA facility inside it was carrying the whole eastern side of the city — a population the project puts at about 180,000.

Boulder raised $170,000 for medical equipment. Cherin told Rocky Mountain PBS in October 2025 that the centre could serve 170,000 people, including 30,000 living in the camps.

On Wednesday 26 November 2025 — a year and a day ago — the Nablus governor, Ghassan Daghlas, opened the Askar Boulder medical dispensary inside Old Askar camp, From the Camp reported. The prime minister's adviser for Arab and Islamic funds, Nasser Qatami, and the energy minister, Ayman Ismail, attended, alongside the popular committees of old and new Askar and of the governorate's other camps.

Daghlas said the project strengthened the camps and gave them health infrastructure that matched a growing need.

The centre holds a laboratory for blood and urine analysis, ultrasound, an X-ray unit, an emergency room, general medicine and a dental unit. The project now reports that the centre runs at near-sustainable levels, covering about 90% of its costs, and lists eleven specialities working out of it.

## A fire truck narrow enough for the alleys

In June the project announced a different kind of delivery. A fire truck it had funded, built deliberately narrow to enter the lanes of the Nablus Old City and the city's refugee camps, had joined the Nablus Municipal Fire Department's fleet.

Nablus has four refugee camps. A standard engine does not fit into them, which in practice means a fire inside a camp burns until it reaches a street wide enough for the fire service to use.

## What the next $150,000 buys

In September, KGNU, the community radio station that covers Boulder and Denver, reported that the project had held a 5K walk to fund the medical centre's expansion. The targets are $100,000 for medical equipment and $50,000 for a children's play yard — in a West Bank where clean outdoor space for children is hard to find.

The walk opened a two-week run of events leading to the United Nations International Day of Peace. The project says a second floor at the medical centre needs $80,000 to $100,000 in construction, and that the play yard is planned for Balata camp, Nablus's largest.

A delegation of Boulder residents spent 14 to 23 November in Palestine. The itinerary, published before they left, put the fire department first — to welcome in the truck — and then the medical centre's staff and the ambulance team.

## What the ledger shows

Nothing in this file is abstract. A camp committee names a specific piece of equipment, a town 11,000 kilometres away pays for exactly that, and the camp supplies what no donor can wire: the volunteers, the roster, the fee that keeps an engine running after the ribbon is cut.

It is a narrow kind of solidarity, and its narrowness is the point. The ledger between Boulder and Askar now reads: one incubator, one intensive-care ambulance, one clinic with eleven specialities, one fire truck that fits.

title: Boulder volunteers gave Askar camp an ambulance and a clinic
